item.title: Kev launches small Jev-like decision models built on Qwen3.5 with pretrained weights and training code [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Kev is a family of compact decision models based on Qwen3.5 and Jev's Architecture Unmasked, offering pretrained weights and the ability to train custom models. It supports yes/no, multiple-choice, and rating questions in a single request, runs on CUDA and Apple Silicon, and includes a web playground for testing inputs and option order effects. The models come in 0.8B, 4B, and 9B parameter sizes, with APIs compatible with TypeSafe's System One Python SDK. Kev-4B and Kev-0.8B can be tried in the browser without installation. The project provides training code, evaluation data, and examples demonstrating how the models handle customer service tickets with probabilistic outputs for department routing, escalation, and customer frustration scoring.

item.title: mini-AGI launches a continual learning language model trainable on a single 8GB VRAM GPU, storing weights on disk to overcome memory limits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: mini-AGI is a byte-level language model designed for continual learning on modest hardware, specifically a single GPU with 8GB VRAM. It dynamically assembles its architecture, trains from scratch, and stores its weights on disk, allowing it to grow capacity and avoid catastrophic forgetting while reading and learning from a continuous data stream. The model uses a unique architecture with adaptive depth and expert routing, enabling it to process characters through multiple recurrent blocks without a fixed layer stack. It is intended as an experiment to demonstrate that personal, continually learning language models can be trained and updated on consumer-grade hardware, with capabilities limited mainly by hardware, data quality, and training time.

item.title: Author advises against using AI to write documents, emphasizing the importance of human thinking in writing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The author recommends not using AI tools like Claude, Codex/ChatGPT, or Gemini for writing because writing requires deep thinking about the problem and communication goals, which AI cannot replicate. While AI can generate text that looks good, it often skips the critical thinking step, resulting in less meaningful content. Instead, the author suggests using AI for tasks like coding, research, data analysis, and improving documents after the initial human writing is done, such as by asking AI to provide feedback or questions rather than generate content from scratch. The article highlights that writing is a tool for thinking and that productivity should focus on the quality and impact of ideas rather than volume. AI can assist in preparing to write by helping sift through and structure data, but the core thinking and writing process should remain human-driven to ensure clarity and depth in communication.

item.description: SpaceXAI has released Grok 4.7, its most powerful AI model designed for coding and knowledge tasks, offering twice the speed and half the price of comparable models. The model features enhanced capabilities for longer, complex tasks, better self-verification, and improved conversational understanding, along with advanced safeguards against misuse. Grok 4.7 is available through Cursor, Grok Build, API access, and third-party platforms, with pricing starting at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens.

item.title: Archestra tests Jev on 100 real agent tool calls to evaluate trust and audience classification accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Archestra conducted an evaluation of Jev, an AI model, on 100 real agent tool calls to assess its ability to classify data trustworthiness and audience scope. The test involved labeling calls based on who can see the output, whether the output is trusted or suspicious, and if calls require trusted sessions or specific audiences. The evaluation compared Jev with other models and analyzed stability, reproducibility, and error types such as false alarms and leaks. The study highlighted challenges like opaque references, outbound data risks, and sensitivity to option order in classification decisions.

item.title: Sources: OpenAI and Anthropic nearly reached a deal to stress-test each other's AI models amid safety concerns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI was negotiating a legally binding agreement with Anthropic to mutually stress-test their AI models as part of its efforts to address safety concerns raised by employees and others. These discussions occurred before recent cybersecurity incidents involving OpenAI's technology and have not been previously reported. The potential deal aimed to enhance AI safety by having the two companies rigorously evaluate each other's systems, reflecting a broader reconsideration of safety strategies within OpenAI in response to growing fears about AI risks.

item.title: Everything Is a Stream: rethinking runtime composability beyond compile-time plugins with stream-based architectures [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: The article argues that the Unix philosophy of "everything is a file" is better understood as "everything is a stream," emphasizing the power of stream processing in computing. It highlights how foundational concepts like Turing machines, TCP, databases, compilers, and large language models fundamentally operate as streams, enabling composability and protocol flexibility. The discussion critiques the "everything is a plugin" approach in software design, especially for autonomous coding agents, noting that while plugin architectures offer malleability at the user interface level, the core system-the "plugged"-requires stability and rigorous verification. The article suggests protecting the core agent engine from unverified plugin changes to maintain reliability, advocating for extending functionality through controlled, stream-based interactions rather than arbitrary plugin injections.

item.title: MIT Technology Review outlines four recommendations to address failures in US border surveillance towers after investigation reveals undetected migrant deaths [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: MIT Technology Review published an investigation revealing that advanced AI-enabled surveillance towers along the US-Mexico border have failed to detect many migrants who later died nearby, exposing systemic flaws such as broken equipment, ineffective algorithms, and unresponsive agents. The report highlights over 1,050 deaths near these towers and calls for urgent reforms in border surveillance practices. The investigation, part of a collaboration with Times of San Diego, found that US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has never conducted a comprehensive audit of the towers' effectiveness or tracked migrant deaths systematically. The report recommends a thorough audit of deaths near the virtual wall, improved tracking of migrant deaths and remains, and better documentation of cases where surveillance technology leads to apprehensions. These steps aim to address the shortcomings in the current $1 billion federal investment to expand the virtual wall by 2034. The findings raise concerns about the accountability and efficacy of border security technology, especially as defense contractor Anduril continues to secure major contracts for new towers. The report underscores the need for CBP to implement data-driven oversight and transparency measures to prevent further loss of life and improve rescue efforts along the border.

item.title: CrowdStrike and Okta trade at high valuation premiums despite limited evidence of AI-driven revenue growth [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Cybersecurity stocks have risen sharply in 2026 as investors anticipate increased demand for defenses against AI-related threats, with the S&P Kensho cybersecurity index up 41% compared to an 11% rise in the S&P 500. However, cloud security firm CrowdStrike and identity security provider Okta have reached valuation highs that may not be justified by their current revenue performance. So far, there is little indication that these companies' growth has been significantly boosted by AI-related concerns, suggesting investors should be cautious about the premium prices.

item.title: Survey finds 60% of companies see AI initiative costs as unpredictable due to token-based pricing, with 64% of budgets spent on software and APIs rather than infrastructure [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A survey of 107 senior leaders reveals that most companies struggle to predict AI spending because token-based pricing varies with usage, complicating budgeting efforts. While 64% of AI budgets go to software, applications, and API models, autonomous AI agents using metered token consumption often cause unexpected expenses. Despite cost challenges, 60% of respondents report increased productivity and over half see AI returns exceeding costs. The survey highlights that traditional per-seat licensing remains common for packaged AI apps, but autonomous agents operating in loops can rapidly increase token consumption and costs. Many companies find it difficult to manage token expenses effectively, with only about a third actively controlling them through strategies like user training and usage caps. Regulatory compliance is also seen as a barrier to adoption, though companies addressing it tend to adopt AI faster. Looking ahead, AI spending is expected to rise as enterprises move beyond experimentation and focus more on cost management and ROI measurement, balancing AI capabilities with traditional software to control expenses and maximize productivity gains.

item.title: Google launches $899 Googlebook laptop with AI-powered Gemini features including AI cursor, dictation, and widgets, available for pre-order with shipments starting October 4 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google has introduced the Googlebook, an AI-native laptop priced at $899 that integrates its Gemini AI capabilities directly into the desktop experience. The device runs on Android OS with Chrome browser elements and features an AI-powered cursor, enhanced dictation called Rambler, and vibe-coded widgets designed to improve user interaction with AI. Google aims to attract users by embedding AI deeply into the laptop rather than relying on separate apps or browser access. The Googlebook targets the education market, potentially replacing Chromebooks used by millions of students and educators, and includes a 12-month subscription to Google AI Pro with cloud storage and advanced Gemini tools. Manufactured by partners like Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, and Lenovo, the device offers up to 14 hours of battery life, high-resolution OLED displays, and dedicated AI processors. Pre-orders are open now with availability in the U.S., Canada, Europe, and Australia starting in early October.

item.title: Google.org commits $4 million to Digital Promise for free AI training for US educators through Google AI Educator Series [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: At the United Nations General Assembly, Google.org announced a $4 million commitment to Digital Promise to provide free, practical AI training for K-12 teachers and higher education faculty across the US. The initiative aims to equip educators with foundational AI skills and instructional strategies through self-paced e-learning modules and digital badges. Digital Promise will develop scalable training models in partnership with state education agencies, school districts, and community colleges to support long-term AI skill development. Over the next two years, it will also research effective AI use in higher education and publish open guides to help institutions adopt AI thoughtfully.

item.title: Google's Co-Scientist AI system generates novel cancer treatment hypotheses by autonomously analyzing scientific literature and synthesizing research [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google's Co-Scientist AI tool autonomously searches, critiques, and synthesizes scientific papers to generate innovative hypotheses, exemplified by its proposal to target cancer protein MYC through molecular condensate manipulation. The system analyzed over 700 papers and suggested a novel approach of gluing protein clusters together to inhibit MYC gene expression, challenging existing strategies. This AI-assisted research method is gaining traction, with other labs and startups developing similar systems to accelerate scientific discovery and shift the role of human researchers toward judgment and decision-making.

item.title: Apple opens claims for $250 million Siri AI settlement covering iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 models purchased between June 2024 and March 2025 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Apple is settling a class action lawsuit for $250 million over allegations it failed to deliver AI-enhanced Siri features promised with the iPhone 16 launch. Eligible US customers who bought an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, can now submit claims for a payout estimated at $25 per device, potentially rising to $95 depending on claim volume. The lawsuit claimed Apple created consumer expectations for AI features previewed at WWDC 2024 that were not available at the iPhone 16 release, which was marketed as "built for Apple Intelligence." The AI-upgraded Siri rollout was delayed until iOS 27 in September 2026. Apple denies any wrongdoing. Claim submissions must be completed by December 21, 2026, via the settlement website.

Liang's most recent remarks, made during a closed-door, in-person meeting on Sunday, came as DeepSeek finalizes its second funding round, which aims to raise 50 billion yuan ($7.5 billion) at a valuation of 500 billion yuan.

"We know where everything is." Why track power so intently? Nvidia sees power availability as a key barrier to getting its AI server chips online as soon as they ship, as we've chronicled in this column over and over. While securing power is the first step to any AI data center project, even before getting the land or chips, developers that work with Google, Microsoft, Oracle and others fear a glut of unused chips due to an eventual power shortage.

item.description: Secretive Wall Street trading firm Jane Street has become famous in the past couple of years for its sizable AI-related spending, as it has struck big cloud deals to handle its AI computing needs and made investments in neocloud CoreWeave. Yet even a Jane Street-related deal for data center debt hasn't won over investors. Debt sold by a venture building a data center to be leased by Jane Street has quickly soured in secondary trading, according to Financial Industry Regulatory Authority data. Yields on the bonds have risen to around 11.3%, more than 2 percentage points above where the debt first sold in August. That deterioration has been sharper than for other recently issued AI data center bonds, with investors demanding far higher compensation to hold them versus government debt.
